key_points.point: Prefill (processing the prompt) is compute-bound / parallel over prompt tokens, and determines time-to-first-token (TTFT).
Decode (generating one token at a time) is memory-bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound, because each step moves the KV cache + weights through memory but does little arithmetic per byte.
The KV cache stores per-layer key/value projections for all tokens generated so far, so attention doesn't need to be recomputed over the whole prefix at every decode step.
KV cache size grows with context length (and layers/heads), competing with model weights for a fixed memory budget -- especially on unified-memory (Apple Silicon) machines.
Speculative decoding proposes several candidate tokens cheaply (a draft), then verifies them all in a single forward pass of the target model, without sacrificing output quality.
MTP (Multi-Token Prediction) attaches extra prediction heads directly to the base model instead of using a separate draft model, so there's no second set of weights to keep in memory.
Acceptance rate (fraction of drafted tokens accepted) is the key metric determining real-world speedup; it varies by workload -- code tends to have higher acceptance rates than free-form prose.

The speedup from a given acceptance rate depends on hardware's compute-to-bandwidth ratio; CUDA GPUs and Apple Silicon/Metal don't necessarily get the same speedup from the same acceptance rate, so it must be measured directly rather than assumed.
